cards.text: This song comes from Asaph, the Levite David made chief of the worship music (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). He opens with a prayer to God. No warm-up, no small talk, friend. He goes STRAIGHT to it.

cards.question: Asaph opens by asking God the same thing three different ways. What is he asking God not to be?

cards.text: "O God, be not silent; be not speechless; be not still, O God." That's me texting "hello?" then "hello??" then "HELLO???" And the three little dots show up and then DISAPPEAR. Pain.
Then Asaph points God to what's going on: "See how Your enemies rage, how Your foes have reared their heads."

cards.question: These raging enemies scheme with cunning. Asaph says they're plotting against God's ___.
The enemies have a plan, and Asaph quotes it. What do they say they want to do to Israel?

cards.text: "Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more." Friend, I spent YEARS forgotten in the back of a junk drawer, and nobody was working THAT hard at it.

cards.question: Asaph says the nations plotting against Israel can't agree on a plan.
These nations plot together with one mind and form an alliance. Who does Asaph say the alliance is against?

cards.text: Then Asaph names who's in on it: Edom, Moab, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre and more, ten names in all. Even Assyria joins, lending strength to the sons of Lot. That's not an alliance, friend. That's a GROUP CHAT, and there's only one topic.

Asaph's got a whole crowd lined up against God's people. So now he pulls out the receipts. OLD ones. He names Midian, the nation God once handed Israel over to for seven years (Judges 6:1), and Sisera, commander of King Jabin's army (Judges 4:2), at the River Kishon.

cards.question: Asaph brings up Midian, Sisera and Jabin. What is he asking God to do to today's enemies?

answers.text: Defeat them like He defeated those enemies
Send them back to their own lands

cards.text: He says they perished at Endor and became like dung on the ground. Then he asks God to make the enemies' leaders like Oreb and Zeeb, princes of Midian (Judges 7:25), and Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian (Judges 8:5).

cards.question: Next Asaph quotes a boast about taking something for themselves. What did they want to possess?

cards.text: Then Asaph trades the history lesson for pictures: "Make them like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind."

cards.question: Tumbleweed and chaff before the wind. Asaph is asking God to make the enemies easy to ___ away.

cards.text: Like crumbs on my counter when I blow on them. FWOOSH. Gone. Then the next picture: fire eating up a forest, and a flame setting the mountains ablaze.

cards.question: After the fire picture, Asaph asks God to chase the enemies down with a flood.

cards.text: Then the prayer takes a turn I did NOT see coming. Asaph asks God to cover their faces with shame, and he says what it's for.

cards.question: Asaph asks God to cover the enemies' faces with shame. Why?

answers.text: So they may seek the LORD's name
So Israel can laugh at them

cards.question: After praying that the enemies seek the LORD's name, Asaph stops asking for them to be ashamed.

cards.text: Next line: "May they be ever ashamed and terrified; may they perish in disgrace." Then comes his very last line, and it's about what he wants them to know.

cards.question: Asaph ends his prayer with what he wants the enemies to know. What is it?

answers.text: That the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth
That Israel will rule over every nation on earth
That Asaph's prayers are always heard in heaven

cards.question: Asaph opened by begging God not to be ___. He closes asking that the enemies ___ the LORD is Most High.

findings.problem: This story card repeats verse 1, which card 1 already set up and card 2 already asked about. It adds a joke but doesn't move the baker forward through the passage.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: In the texting joke, God is the one who starts to reply ("the three little dots show up") and then backs out ("DISAPPEAR. Pain."). That puts God in the punchline. It also adds an action the verse doesn't have: the verse is about silence, not a reply that starts and stops.

rule.text: His humor never targets God, Jesus, Scripture or the Marriage Supper.

findings.problem: Two wrong answers carry limiting words ("Asaph alone", "The priests only") that make them easy to rule out, and "Asaph alone" reads as silly. "God Himself" stands out as the right answer.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The card says "ten names in all" and then "Even Assyria joins." That reads as if Assyria comes on top of the ten, which would make eleven. Verses 6-8 name ten groups with Assyria included, so the wording misstates the count.

rule.text: Noticing: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences. Only the opening card of the passage can go past 2 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card is a dense list of four names with two outside references, and none of Papa Dorin's voice. It reads like a reference note, not the storyteller.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The question asks "What did they want to possess?", where "they" points back to a card the baker can no longer see. It never says who made the boast: the nobles and princes Asaph just named, like Zebah and Zalmunna.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: Verse 15 only shows up as a false statement (a flood). No card ever tells the baker what Asaph actually asks: that God pursue them with His tempest and terrify them with His storm, as the "so" that completes the fire picture in verse 14. The baker leaves without that detail.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: This card is a recap. Blank 1 ("silent") asks verse 1 again, which stop 1 card 2 already tested. Blank 2 ("know") repeats what cards 12 and 13 just covered. The card doesn't move the passage forward.

The card says the Asaph of this psalm's title is the Levite David made chief of the worship music (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). The title says only "A Psalm of Asaph." Psalm 83 is often thought to come from a later time or from Asaph's descendants, and the passage doesn't confirm which.
findings.question: When a psalm title names Asaph, should Papa Dorin say he is David's chief musician from 1 Chronicles 16, or keep it open and just say the song comes from Asaph?
